orderWasChangedOnPurposeAndItPaidOff.whatTheCoordinatorAsked: 1) threshold 30, 2) retire two unreachable promises, 3) raise #76, 4) rebase the checks.
orderWasChangedOnPurposeAndItPaidOff.why: The coordinator's own principle for this round was «first everything that moves the party, then the rebasing», and retiring a promise does not move the party while #76 does. Retiring a promise as unreachable BEFORE the change that might make it reachable would have been the same mistake as re-pinning a check under a moving target.
orderWasChangedOnPurposeAndItPaidOff.andItWasNotHypothetical: The memory-of-place observability floor on `prepared` — one of the two promises queued for retirement — was 0 refusals over the matrix at threshold 30 without #76. With #76 it is 8, against a floor of 10. It went from «unreachable, retire it» to «two short». That promise must NOT be retired on the old measurement, and the decision has to be taken again on the party as it now is.

whatWasImplementedForIssue76.scopeTaken: Cell occupancy in pathfinding, and nothing else.
whatWasImplementedForIssue76.theFindingThatMadeItSmall: Occupancy already existed at the moment of stepping: `Move` has always refused to put a creature on a tile another one occupies. What did not exist was the pathfinder knowing it. So a creature walked into a body, was refused, and walked into it again the next tick — which is exactly the jam this slice created. The fix is that bodies now join the same blocked set the forbidden zone already uses, so `NextStep` routes around them.
whatWasImplementedForIssue76.theBoundKept: «A body takes away a road and never the objective» — the same bound the issue's own recommendation and the existing raider-memory code already carry. No way round means the crowded path is used and the step-time check does the waiting. The destination tile is never treated as occupied for a creature, because creatures are routinely sent to a tile somebody stands on.
whatWasImplementedForIssue76.raiders: Criterion 1 of #76 — raiders no longer share a cell. Same blocked-set mechanism plus a hard step-time check. Here the destination IS blocked, deliberately: every raider of a wave walks to the same larder tile, so exempting the destination would have exempted precisely the tile the owner watched them pile onto.

criterion2WasNotAFormality.claim: The wait limit that criterion 2 asks for is what keeps the party finishing, not a nicety.
criterion2WasNotAFormality.measured: Implemented without it first. Result: the queue behind an occupied larder never drained, no wave after the first resolved, parties ran to SessionTicks with a null outcome («The party did not end (outcome null, unresolved False)»), and the simulation suite went to about fifteen red including the byte-for-byte replay check. `RaiderBlockedPatience` = 4 removes it and the suite returns to six.
criterion2WasNotAFormality.whereTheReasonLives: beside the constant in PrototypeTuning, with the measurement.

whatWasImplementedForIssue76.whatWasLeftOfIssue76: The choice between its variants A/B/C as a general rule for all bodies; the corridor-as-throat gameplay consequences; criterion 5 (a headless scenario showing a narrow corridor changes a wave outcome); line of sight; and the contract section on resolution order. Taken: occupancy in pathfinding, criterion 1, criterion 2. This split is owed a section in the pull-request body.
